summary: Discusses implementation issues when providing compulsory tunneling in dial-up networks, where the network operator rather than the user sets up an L2TP tunnel, with RADIUS used for authentication and configuration. It is an informational memo.

eli5.summary: When you dial in to a service, the company can decide to send your connection through a private pipe to the right place. This describes how that choice gets made and passed along.

questions: how does radius set up an l2tp tunnel
what is the difference between lac and lns
subtitle: How a dial-up access server, RADIUS and an L2TP tunnel server work together to send a user down a tunnel they never asked for.

tldr.problem: Some dial-up services need every user sent to a specific host through a tunnel, without the user doing anything. Static and realm-based tunneling are inflexible, and the details of authenticating the user in this setup are tricky.
tldr.mechanism: The Network Access Server (NAS) asks a RADIUS server about the caller. The RADIUS reply carries tunnel attributes, and the NAS then builds an L2TP tunnel to the tunnel server, which finishes PPP negotiation and assigns the address.
tldr.outcome: The RFC compares single and dual authentication, describes start-up and tear-down sequences, and gives security rules. It is an informational memo.

today: RFC 2809 is an Informational memo from April 2000. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it builds on the L2TP and RADIUS specifications of its time (RFC 2661 and RFC 2138).

sections.title: Compulsory Tunneling and Why Use RADIUS
sections.content:
In voluntary tunneling the user creates the tunnel, usually with a tunneling client. In compulsory tunneling the tunnel is created without any action from the user and without giving the user any choice. Examples named in the RFC are software upgrade servers, software registration servers and banking services, which need to limit users to specific hosts.

The RFC argues for RADIUS-based, user-based tunneling over two alternatives. Static tunneling sends all users to one endpoint and needs a dedicated NAS. Realm-based tunneling picks the endpoint from the realm in the userID, so everyone in a realm is treated alike. With RADIUS, an account can be given its own tunnel server: the RFC's example is one employee tunneled to an engineering department server and another to a sales department server.

The new RADIUS attributes that carry tunnel information are defined in a separate work in progress, not in this document.
sections.eli5: Sometimes a company wants every caller sent straight to one special place. RADIUS lets it decide for each person, not just for everyone at once.

sections.title: The Players
sections.content:
Four roles appear throughout:

  • NAS (Network Access Server): the device clients contact to reach the network. In L2TP terms, a NAS doing compulsory tunneling is the L2TP Access Concentrator (LAC).
  • Tunnel server: terminates the tunnel. In L2TP it is the L2TP Network Server (LNS).
  • RADIUS server: provides authentication and authorization, using the protocol of RFC 2138.
  • RADIUS proxy: looks like a server to the NAS and like a client to the server, and can help locate the tunnel endpoint.

The tunnel protocol here is L2TP, defined in RFC 2661. Other tunneling protocols are left to separate documents.
sections.eli5: The caller dials a front desk (the NAS). A phone book (RADIUS) says where the caller should go, and the front desk builds a private pipe to that office (the tunnel server).

sections.title: Single and Dual Authentication
sections.content:
The RFC separates single authentication, where the user is authenticated once, from dual authentication, where both the NAS and the tunnel server authenticate the user.

  • NAS authentication: the user is authenticated and authorized once, at the NAS. This blocks unauthorized users and allows accounting at the NAS, but the tunnel server must trust the NAS and cannot strongly verify who is billed. It is not compatible with roaming.
  • NAS authentication with RADIUS reply forwarding: the RADIUS reply is forwarded to the tunnel server, which then needs the shared secret. The RFC calls this impractical, because with a RADIUS proxy the reply is authenticated with the secret shared by the client and proxy.
  • Tunnel server authentication: the NAS decides, from RADIUS or its own configuration, that the user needs a tunnel, and only the tunnel server authenticates. The decision can use the Calling-Station-Id and Called-Station-Id attributes (telephone-number based) or the userID, such as its domain portion or attribute-specific processing. This approach is also incompatible with roaming.
  • Dual authentication: accounting at both ends and compatible with roaming, but the client must handle two rounds of authentication and possibly LCP renegotiation, and some clients do not support it. Feasible combinations include PAP/PAP(token), PAP/CHAP, PAP/EAP, CHAP/PAP(token), CHAP/CHAP, CHAP/EAP, EAP/CHAP and EAP/EAP.
sections.eli5: Do you show your ticket once at the front desk, only at the final office, or at both? Each choice has good and bad points for who trusts whom and who can send the bill.

sections.title: Setting Up and Tearing Down the Tunnel
sections.content:
In every variant the NAS sends a RADIUS Access-Request, receives an Access-Accept with tunnel attributes (or an Access-Reject), and, if a tunnel is indicated, brings up an L2TP control connection if none exists. It does that with Start-Control-Connection-Request, then sends Incoming-Call-Request, gets Incoming-Call-Reply and answers with Incoming-Call-Connected. Data then flows through the tunnel.

The NAS typically uses LCP forwarding, though the tunnel server can renegotiate LCP. If renegotiation is to be allowed, the NAS SHOULD NOT send an LCP CONFACK completing negotiation, and the client and NAS MUST NOT begin NCP negotiation. NCP negotiation happens between the client and the tunnel server, which assigns the address. With telephone-number based authentication, the NAS MUST NOT begin PPP authentication before bringing up the tunnel, and L2TP authentication forwarding MUST NOT be used. If the access is rejected, or the control connection or call setup reports an error, the NAS MUST send an LCP-Terminate and disconnect the user.

Tear-down is nearly the same in all cases. If the client ends the session, the tunnel server MUST end PPP and send Call-Clear-Request, and the NAS MUST answer with Call-Disconnect-Notify and disconnect. For a line problem or hangup the NAS MUST send Call-Disconnect-Notify, and both sides tear down the call.
sections.eli5: The front desk checks with the phone book, builds the pipe, and hands the caller over. When the call ends, both sides say goodbye and close the pipe.

sections.title: Distinct RADIUS Servers and UserIDs
sections.content:
When the NAS and the tunnel server use different RADIUS servers, they likely need different userID and password pairs. Forwarding authentication information in the L2TP setup would then make tunnel authentication fail, so where user-based tunneling via RADIUS is used, L2TP authentication forwarding SHOULD NOT be employed. Clients often try the first pair again, and the RFC prefers asking for the second pair rather than showing an authentication error. One-time passwords make this need clearer.

For Multilink PPP, the two RADIUS servers may return different Port-Limit attributes. If the tunnel server allows more channels, the client should open a connection to another NAS to bring up a bundle, and MUST NOT tell that NAS the link is part of a multilink bundle. If the tunnel allows fewer, the client should end use of the excess channels.

Using RADIUS means the userID no longer has double duty. It routes the RADIUS request only, and the returned tunnel attributes pick the tunnel endpoint.
sections.eli5: If two offices keep separate guest lists, you may need two different passwords, so the system should ask you for the second one instead of just saying no.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
In PPP-based tunneling the client cannot tell it is tunneled, so PPP security is negotiated between the client and the tunnel server over the whole path. For L2TP this includes PPP encryption and compression. The NAS may also set up an IPSEC security association with the tunnel server for added protection.

RADIUS proxies that forward the Access-Reply MUST NOT modify tunnel attributes. A proxy that does not support tunnel attributes MUST send an Access-Reject to the NAS, so access is only granted if the requested services can be provided. If tunnel attributes are present, the NAS MUST ignore any address assignment attributes from the RADIUS server and MUST NOT begin NCP negotiation, because that could open a window in which the client can send packets to the transport network, which compulsory tunneling does not permit.
sections.eli5: Nobody in the middle may change the instructions for where to send the caller, and the caller must not get loose on the open network before reaching the right place.
